cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 8.1, p. 154. Dexamethasone is ~25× hydrocortisone and has no mineralocorticoid effect, hence its use for tumor edema.

cards.rueckseite:
Normal adrenal output under stress: **≈ 250–300 mg hydrocortisone/day**.
- **Mild illness** (cold, UTI, single tooth extraction): **double** the daily dose
- **Moderate stress** (flu, minor surgery under local): **50 mg hydrocortisone BID**
- **Major illness, severe trauma, emergency surgery under GA:** **100 mg hydrocortisone IV q 6–8 h** for 3–4 days

Applies to anyone on chronic glucocorticoids now or within the last **1–2 years**.

cards.text: Steroid taper: baseline adrenal function has returned when the **8 AM cortisol** (before the morning dose) is {{c1::> 10 mcg/dL}}. Stress doses are still needed until a {{c2::cosyntropin stimulation test}} is normal; the risk of adrenal insufficiency persists for about {{c3::2 years}} after stopping chronic steroids.

cards.vorderseite: Steroid side effects relevant to neurosurgery
cards.rueckseite:
- **CNS:** steroid psychosis, **spinal epidural lipomatosis** (cord compression, rare), pseudotumor cerebri (on withdrawal), PML
- **Endocrine/metabolic:** hyperglycemia, HPA-axis suppression → adrenal crisis on withdrawal, growth suppression in children
- **Cardiovascular/renal:** hypertension, Na/water retention, hypokalemic alkalosis
- **GI:** gastritis/ulcer (risk mainly > 3 weeks or very high doses), perforation can be masked
- **Musculoskeletal:** osteoporosis, **avascular necrosis** of the femoral head, steroid myopathy
- Impaired wound healing, immunosuppression

Replace **glucocorticoids before (or with) thyroid hormone**. Thyroid replacement alone increases cortisol metabolism and can precipitate an **adrenal crisis**. In myxedema coma give ≈ 300–400 mg hydrocortisone IV/24 h together with thyroid replacement.

Emergency of hypothyroidism, **≈ 50% mortality**.
**Signs:** altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypotension, **hyponatremia**, hypoglycemia, hypoventilation, sometimes seizures.
**Treatment:** IV thyroid hormone (gut absorption poor) + **hydrocortisone**; supportive care (fluids, glucose, ventilation). Hyponatremia corrects with thyroid replacement, so **avoid hypertonic saline**. Hypotension responds poorly to pressors until thyroid is replaced.

cards.titel: Diabetes insipidus after pituitary or stalk injury: three patterns
zeilen: Polyuria/polydipsia that normalizes within ≈ 12–36 h after surgery
Lasts months or is permanent; ≈ 2/3 return to near normal by 1 year (ADH released directly from the hypothalamus)
1) DI for 4–5 days (reduced ADH) → 2) ADH released from dying cells for 4–5 days → normo- or **hyponatremia (SIADH-like)** → 3) DI again (transient or permanent)
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 125. Danger in phase 2: continuing vasopressin causes iatrogenic SIADH, so use short-acting agents and re-dose only on recurrence of polyuria.

cards.text: Clinical central DI appears only after about {{c1::85%}} of ADH secretory capacity is lost. Craniopharyngioma rarely causes DI **before** surgery because {{c2::the hypothalamic nuclei can still produce and release ADH}}; pituitary macroadenomas cause DI {{c3::rarely (except with apoplexy)}}.

cards.rueckseite:
Renal resistance to ADH (no response to DDAVP):
- Familial (X-linked recessive)
- **Hypokalemia**, **hypercalcemia**
- Drugs: **lithium**, demeclocycline, colchicine
- Chronic renal disease (pyelonephritis, amyloidosis, sickle cell, polycystic kidneys), Sjögren

Also exclude osmotic diuresis (mannitol, glucosuria) and diuretics.

cards.text: **Free water deficit** = {{c1::0.6 × body weight (kg) × ([Na]current / 140 − 1)}}. Replace {{c2::half}} of the deficit over the first 24 h and the rest over the next {{c3::1–2 days}} to avoid cerebral edema.

**Pseudohyponatremia / translocational hyponatremia:** for every 100 mg/dL rise in glucose, serum Na falls by {{c1::1.6–2.4 mEq/L}}. Other osmotically active causes: {{c2::mannitol}}. Lab artifact with normal osmolality: {{c3::hyperlipidemia or hyperproteinemia}}.

cards.rueckseite:
**Features:** metabolic acidosis, **hyperkalemia**, rhabdomyolysis, lipemia, hepatomegaly, myocardial failure, renal failure, death.
**Risk:** doses **> 50 mcg/kg/min** or any dose **> 48 h** (first described in children).
Rule: unexplained metabolic acidosis on propofol is PRIS until proven otherwise → stop propofol.
Also: lipid carrier gives 1.1 kcal/mL (hypertriglyceridemia); change bottle/tubing every 12 h.

**α2-agonist** acting in the locus coeruleus: sedation + analgesia with **little respiratory depression**, patient stays arousable (good for **awake craniotomy** and as a transition drug), reduces shivering and opioid need.
Dose: load 1 mcg/kg over 10 min (optional), then **0.2–1.0 mcg/kg/h**.
Main side effects: **bradycardia, sinus arrest**, hypotension.

- **Naloxone** (opioids): titrate 0.04–0.4 mg IV; short half-life, so re-sedation is possible; abrupt full reversal can cause hypertension, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias
- **Flumazenil** (benzodiazepines): can provoke **seizures** (especially chronic benzodiazepine use or tricyclic overdose) and raise ICP; short duration
- Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium; neostigmine + glycopyrrolate for other nondepolarizers

cards.text: Circulating blood volume: premature infant {{c1::85–100 mL/kg}}, term infant < 1 month {{c2::85 mL/kg}}, older than 1 month incl. adults {{c3::75 mL/kg}}. A massive transfusion is replacement of > {{c4::1 blood volume in 24 h}} (adult), requiring platelets and FFP.

cards.rueckseite:
- Recent severe head injury or recent craniotomy
- Coagulopathy, hemorrhagic infarction
- Bleeding ulcer or other inaccessible bleeding site
- Uncontrolled hypertension
- Severe hepatic or renal disease
- < 4–6 h before an invasive procedure
- (Brain tumor: relative; several studies show no excess bleeding)

Massive PE with hemodynamic compromise is usually anticoagulated despite intracranial risk.

- **Full anticoagulation:** most wait **≥ 3–5 days** (some 2 weeks); one study found no excess bleeding from day 3. Higher risk after parenchymal surgery (tumor) than after aneurysm clipping.
- **Prophylactic dose:** heparin **5000 U SQ** 2 h preop and q 12 h postop, or enoxaparin 40 mg SQ daily (one RCT: 11% postop hemorrhage with enoxaparin)
- Mechanical prophylaxis (SCDs/stockings) from the start

cards.titel: DVT risk and prophylaxis in neurosurgical patients
zeilen: ≥ 40 yrs, malignancy, bed rest, surgery > 30 min, SAH, head injury
SCD/stockings; mini-dose heparin if no ICH/SAH
cards.notiz: Greenberg Table 9.8, p. 177. PE risk after supratentorial tumor craniotomy ≈ 7% vs. ≈ 0% after posterior fossa tumors.

cards.text: Clinical diagnosis of DVT is unreliable: a patient with the classic hot, swollen, tender calf or positive {{c1::Homans' sign}} has a DVT only {{c2::20–50%}} of the time, and {{c3::50–60%}} of DVTs have none of these findings. Diagnostic test of choice: {{c4::compression duplex ultrasound}}.

zeilen: ≥ 48 h for high bleeding risk (longer if CrCl < 30)
48–72 h if CrCl > 50; up to 96 h if CrCl 30–50 (renally cleared)
cards.notiz: Greenberg Tables 9.4–9.6, p. 165–171. Neurosurgery counts as high bleeding risk. Patients with fresh drug-eluting coronary stents: discuss with cardiology before stopping dual antiplatelet therapy.

cards.rueckseite:
After long bone fracture (usually femur), **12–72 h** after injury.
**Triad:** respiratory failure (bilateral fluffy infiltrates, hypoxemia), **global neurologic dysfunction** (confusion out of proportion to PaO₂, seizures), **petechial rash** (thorax, axilla, conjunctiva, 24–72 h).
No specific test (fat in urine, BAL with > 5% fat-laden cells). MRI: multiple small DWI dots ("starfield").
**Treatment:** supportive (O₂, PEEP); early fracture fixation reduces incidence; steroids controversial. Mortality ≈ 10%.

**Signs:** sudden dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, pleuritic pain; ECG often only sinus tachycardia (S1Q3T3 rare).
**Diagnosis:** CT pulmonary angiography; duplex of the legs.
**Treatment:** anticoagulation if not contraindicated; when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g., fresh craniotomy, ICH) → **IVC filter**; massive PE with shock → anticoagulation/thrombolysis despite intracranial risk.

Hyperglycemia worsens outcome after stroke, SAH, TBI and increases infection risk (steroids are a common cause). Target roughly **140–180 mg/dL** in the ICU; avoid **hypoglycemia** (tight control < 110 increased mortality in NICE-SUGAR). Correct serum Na for glucose (+1.6–2.4 per 100 mg/dL).

cards.text: Hyperkalemia after **succinylcholine** is a risk in patients with {{c1::denervation (spinal cord injury, stroke), burns, crush injury or prolonged immobilization}}, starting about {{c2::24–72 h}} after the injury, because of {{c3::upregulated extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors}}. Use a nondepolarizing agent (e.g., rocuronium) instead.
